content: Similarly, outcomes related to cardiovascular death, cognitive impairment, dementia, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and end-stage kidney disease were also not reported in many cases. Several trials contributing significant weight to pooled estimates were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias. This was due to issues such as inadequate allocation concealment, lack of blinding of participants and personnel, incomplete outcome data, and selective reporting. For example, trials with over 50% of the pooled estimate weight were often at high risk of bias in these domains. Confidence intervals (CIs) frequently crossed the line of no effect, indicating uncertainty about whether the interventions had a meaningful benefit or harm. In some cases, the lower end of the CI suggested a potential benefit, while the upper end suggested harm, leading to conflicting interpretations. This variability in effect estimates was often accompanied by high statistical heterogeneity, as reflected by I-squared values exceeding 50% in many analyses. In head-to-head comparisons of first-line antihypertensive agents (e.g., beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs), evidence was assessed for both desirable and undesirable effects. However, the certainty of evidence was often rated as low or very low due to methodological limitations, including high risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision in the results. Some trials, such as the ALLHAT 2002 and LIFE trials, contributed a large proportion of the pooled estimates (e.g., >70-80%) but were judged to have unclear or high risk of bias in domains such as allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome assessment. This further reduced the reliability of the findings. In network meta-analyses, included trials often had unclear risks of selection bias (e.g., random sequence generation and allocation concealment) and attrition bias. Additionally, some analyses combined placebo and active treatment comparators, which may have introduced further inconsistency. Baseline risks and event rates were frequently not reported or imputed from other trials, limiting the ability to draw robust conclusions. In some cases, the lack of detailed risk of bias assessments or forest plots further complicated the interpretation of results. Overall, the evidence for the comparative effectiveness and safety of antihypertensive agents remains uncertain due to methodological limitations, high heterogeneity, and imprecision in the available data. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify the benefits and harms of these treatments in adults with hypertension requiring pharmacological intervention.
